name: greek-and-roman-gods

description.en: 43 cards on 22 Greek gods: the twelve Olympians (counting both Hestia and Dionysus, as lists differ), Hades, Persephone, Eros, Cronus and five personified gods such as Helios and Nike. One kind of card asks for the god's Roman counterpart (Zeus → Jupiter), the other for what the god is god of (Zeus → the sky and thunder), in English and Swedish. Correspondences, names and domains from Wikidata and the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica, in our own words, checked against the Theoi Project and Swedish Wikipedia.
description.sv: 43 kort om 22 grekiska gudar: de tolv olympierna (både Hestia och Dionysos medräknade, eftersom listorna skiljer sig åt), Hades, Persefone, Eros, Kronos och fem personifierade gudar som Helios och Nike. Den ena sortens kort frågar efter gudens romerska motsvarighet (Zeus → Jupiter), den andra efter vad guden är gud för (Zeus → himlen och åskan), på engelska och svenska. Motsvarigheter, namn och gudarnas områden från Wikidata och Encyclopædia Britannica från 1911, med egna ord, kontrollerade mot Theoi Project och svenska Wikipedia.

eb1911.title: Encyclopædia Britannica, 11th edition (1911), as transcribed on Wikisource
eb1911.creator: Hugh Chisholm (editor) and the Encyclopædia Britannica's contributors; transcription by Wikisource contributors
eb1911.licenseEvidence: https://en.wikisource.org/wiki/1911_Encyclop%C3%A6dia_Britannica — licence notice on the page: "This work is in the public domain in the United States because it was published before January 1, 1931. This work may be in the public domain in countries and areas with longer native copyright terms that apply the rule of the shorter term to foreign works." Published 1910–1911. Outside the US: the articles used are either unsigned (Poseidon, Ares, Hestia, Dionysus, Pluto, Cupid, Eros (god), Liber and Libera, and the anonymous part of Proserpine), so anonymous works published over 70 years ago, or by contributors who died more than 70 years ago (Zeus: Lewis Richard Farnell, d. 1934; Hera, Hephaestus, Hermes: Edward Ernest Sikes, d. 1940; Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Aphrodite: John Henry Freese, d. 1930; Proserpine: James George Frazer, d. 1941; Fortuna: William Warde Fowler, d. 1921; signatures from the Wikisource headers and the articles' initials, death dates from Wikidata, query 15), and only facts, no text, were taken from them.
eb1911.usedFor: The domains of Apollo (music, prophecy and healing), for which Wikidata has no domain statement, of Persephone (the underworld and spring vegetation, article "Proserpine") the note on Dionysus (article "Dionysus") and confirmation of Eros as god of love (article "Eros (god)"); the Roman names Pluto (with Dis Pater and Orcus), Proserpina, Cupid/Amor, Bacchus/Liber and Fortuna (articles "Pluto", "Proserpine", "Cupid", "Liber and Libera", "Fortuna"); and an independent check of the correspondences and domains of the Olympians (articles Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, Hestia; the article Dionysus names no Roman counterpart, which comes from "Liber and Libera").

theoi.creator: Aaron J. Atsma

theoi.usedFor: Verification only: each god's page (its title line names the Roman counterpart, its first paragraph the god's domains) was used to confirm every card. No selection was taken from it, and no answer rests on it alone. Two short factual answers coincide with its title lines (Athena "wisdom, war and crafts"; formerly also Dionysus "wine and festivity", changed after review rounds 1 and 3); every element of the Athena answer comes from Wikidata (see the card).

sv-wikipedia.usedFor: Verification only: that the Swedish names on the cards are the established ones (article titles and first sentences), and an independent check of each correspondence and domain. The Swedish name Dionysos (missing as a Wikidata label, taken from Wikidata's Swedish Wikipedia sitelink title) was confirmed in the article. No text and no selection was taken from it.

method: Who did the work: Anton Wiklund compiled this deck with the help of AI agents (Claude, by Anthropic), which did the research, drafting and cross-checking at his direction. The cards were checked by machine (live Wikidata and the app's SHACL and DCAT-AP validators) and in independent review rounds by further Claude agents, each logged under Quality control with its findings and how they were resolved. Anton Wiklund reviews every deck in full before it is released.

Finding the right Wikidata property. The brief suggested P2959, which is "permanent duplicated item" and does not link gods. The statements of Zeus (Q34201) were listed (query 1); the Greek–Roman correspondences are recorded with P460 "said to be the same as" (Zeus → Jupiter Q4649) and the god's domains with P2925 "domain of saint or deity".

Candidates. The twelve Olympians (Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, and both Hestia and Dionysus, since lists of the twelve differ on these two), plus Hades, Persephone, Eros and Cronus, and the personified gods Helios, Selene, Eos, Nike and Tyche, whose Roman counterparts are one-to-one. Their P460 values with English and Swedish labels were fetched with query 2; Eros, Helios, Nike and Dionysus were looked up by their English Wikipedia sitelinks (API call 4), and the labels, aliases and Swedish sitelinks of all Greek and Roman items with API call 5.

Choosing the counterpart. P460 often lists several equivalents (Zeus: Jupiter, Thor, Amun, Indra and others). For each god the Roman deity among the P460 values was taken; where two Roman gods were listed (Hades: Pluto and Dis Pater; Dionysus: Bacchus and Liber; Persephone: Proserpina and Libera; Selene: Luna and Diana; Eros: Cupid via Q5011), the choice was made from the content sources and the other is mentioned in a note where it is common: Pluto, whose Wikidata description is "god in Roman religion, Plouton in Greek" and of whom the 1911 Britannica ("Pluto") says that among the Romans Hades "was usually called Dis pater ... and Orcus, although the name Pluto is often used" (so the card states this convention in its note); Bacchus, "ancient Roman deity of wine" in Wikidata, which the 1911 Britannica ("Liber and Libera") gives as another name of Liber; Proserpina, "the Latin form of Persephone" (1911 Britannica, "Proserpine"), Libera being only "sometimes identified" with her; Luna, "Roman goddess of the Moon" in Wikidata, Diana being Artemis's counterpart; Cupid, "Roman deity, counterpart of Eros" in Wikidata and "the Latin name for the god of love, Eros" in the 1911 Britannica ("Cupid"). The Theoi title lines agree with every choice but did not decide any (as first drafted, this step used them as the tie-break; changed in review round 3).

Names on the cards. English names are the Wikidata English labels (Cronus, Hephaestus, Mercury, Vulcan, Neptune, Saturn, Cupid). Swedish names are the Wikidata Swedish labels (Afrodite, Hefaistos, Persefone, Kronos, Apollon, Mercurius, Vulcanus, Neptunus, Saturnus, Amor), except where Wikidata had none: Dionysus (Q41680) has no Swedish label (only the misspelt alias "Dinosys"), so "Dionysos" was taken from the item's Swedish Wikipedia sitelink title recorded in Wikidata (API call 5, CC0) and confirmed in the article itself; Sol (Q1199937) has the Swedish label "Sol Indiges" and the alias "Sol", and "Sol" was used. Each Swedish name was confirmed against the Swedish Wikipedia article (API calls 9–11).

Domains. The domains of each god were taken from Wikidata (P2925 values with their English and Swedish labels, queries 3a and 3b, and the items' English descriptions) and written as a short phrase in our own words in English and Swedish, keeping only the god's main, uncontested domains. Apollo has no P2925 statement and is typed only as a "solar deity", a late identification; his domains (music, prophecy and healing) were taken from the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica article (fetched from Wikisource, API call 7). Persephone has no P2925 statement and Wikidata describes her only as goddess of the seasons and queen of the underworld; her answer (the underworld and spring vegetation) follows the 1911 Britannica article "Proserpine" (query 14). The Dionysus answer is "wine" (Wikidata P2925), with his vegetation aspect and ecstatic worship from the 1911 Britannica article in a note; the Tyche answer is "fortune", Wikidata's description (both shortened in review rounds 1 and 3, see there). Swedish answers name the domains in the definite form ("kriget", "kärleken och skönheten"), as Swedish names a god's domain with a definite genitive ("krigets gud"). No domain card was written for Cronus (see selection).

Cross-checking. Every card was compared with the god's Theoi Project page (fetched with query 6: the title line "… (Roman X)" and the first paragraph "X was the god of …"), with the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica articles (query 7 for the Olympians, query 14 for Pluto, Proserpine, Cupid, Liber and Libera and Fortuna) and with the first paragraph of the Swedish Wikipedia article (API calls 9–11). All sources agree on every correspondence and domain on the cards, except that the 1911 Britannica's article Dionysus names no Roman counterpart (its article "Liber and Libera" does) and that it says the Romans usually called Hades Dis pater or Orcus (see the note on hades-roman); differences in emphasis are recorded in the quality-control log.

The dossier's Wikidata checks (English and Swedish labels of every Greek and Roman god on the cards, the P460 link for every correspondence and P2925 values for the domains) are run by the builder against live Wikidata on every build.
selection: The deck covers the twelve Olympians (counting both Hestia and Dionysus, since ancient lists differ on which of the two belongs to the twelve), Hades, Persephone, Eros and Cronus, and five personified gods with a single standard Roman counterpart: Helios (Sol), Selene (Luna), Eos (Aurora), Nike (Victoria) and Tyche (Fortuna). Each god has a card asking for the Roman counterpart; each except Cronus has a card asking for the god's domains. Left out: gods with no single standard Roman counterpart (Gaia: Terra or Tellus; Hecate; Pan: Faunus is only partly equivalent; Uranus; Rhea: Ops or Cybele) and minor gods; the domain card for Cronus, because the common description of him as god of time comes from an ancient confusion of Kronos with Chronos, and he is better described as king of the Titans than as a god of something. Domains are limited to each god's main, generally agreed ones; later or contested identifications (Apollo as sun god, Artemis as moon goddess) are left out of the answers and mentioned in a note where helpful.

3a. The P2925 "domain of saint or deity" values of the candidates, with English and Swedish labels.

6. Fetch each god's Theoi Project page (Python script, User-Agent "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)", one second between requests) and extract the title line and first paragraph.
queries.query:
URLs: https://www.theoi.com/ + Olympios/Zeus.html, Olympios/Hera.html, Olympios/Poseidon.html, Olympios/Demeter.html, Olympios/Athena.html, Olympios/Apollon.html, Olympios/Artemis.html, Olympios/Ares.html, Olympios/Aphrodite.html, Olympios/Hephaistos.html, Olympios/Hermes.html, Ouranios/Hestia.html, Olympios/Dionysos.html, Khthonios/Haides.html, Khthonios/Persephone.html, Ouranios/Eros.html, Titan/TitanKronos.html, Titan/Helios.html, Titan/Selene.html, Titan/Eos.html, Daimon/Nike.html, Daimon/Tykhe.html

Script run (python3 fetch_theoi.py). The title line is the page's text before the first paragraph; the first paragraph is the text around the first " was " in the tag-stripped page ("intro" in summary.json):

import re, time, urllib.request, html, json
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path(__file__).parent / "theoi"
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
PAGES = {
    "zeus": "Olympios/Zeus.html", "hera": "Olympios/Hera.html", "poseidon": "Olympios/Poseidon.html",
    "demeter": "Olympios/Demeter.html", "athena": "Olympios/Athena.html", "apollo": "Olympios/Apollon.html",
    "artemis": "Olympios/Artemis.html", "ares": "Olympios/Ares.html", "aphrodite": "Olympios/Aphrodite.html",
    "hephaestus": "Olympios/Hephaistos.html", "hermes": "Olympios/Hermes.html", "hestia": "Ouranios/Hestia.html",
    "dionysus": "Olympios/Dionysos.html", "hades": "Khthonios/Haides.html", "persephone": "Khthonios/Persephone.html",
    "eros": "Ouranios/Eros.html", "cronus": "Titan/TitanKronos.html", "helios": "Titan/Helios.html",
    "selene": "Titan/Selene.html", "eos": "Titan/Eos.html", "nike": "Daimon/Nike.html", "tyche": "Daimon/Tykhe.html",
}
UA = "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)"
summary = {}
for key, path in PAGES.items():
    url = "https://www.theoi.com/" + path
    try:
        req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA})
        raw = urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60).read().decode("utf-8", "replace")
    except Exception as e:
        summary[key] = {"url": url, "error": str(e)}
        continue
    (OUT / f"{key}.html").write_text(raw, encoding="utf-8")
    text = html.unescape(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", raw))
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", text)
    i = text.find(" was ")
    roman = [m.group(0) for m in re.finditer(r".{0,120}(?:Roman|Latin).{0,160}", text)][:4]
    summary[key] = {"url": url, "intro": text[max(0, i - 80): i + 600], "roman": roman}
    time.sleep(1)
(OUT / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")

queries.purpose: 7. Fetch the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica articles from Wikisource (Python script, one request per title, one second apart). Hades, Persephone, Eros, Cronus, Helios, Selene, Eos, Nike and Tyche have no article under these titles; Hades, Persephone and Eros are covered under their Latin names Pluto, Proserpine and Cupid, which were first fetched in review (query 14).
queries.query:
https://en.wikisource.org/w/api.php?action=parse&page=1911 Encyclopædia Britannica/{title}&prop=text&format=json&formatversion=2&redirects=1 for title in Zeus, Hera, Poseidon, Demeter, Athena, Apollo, Artemis, Ares, Aphrodite, Hephaestus, Hermes, Hestia, Dionysus, Hades, Persephone, Eros, Cronus, Helios, Selene, Eos, Nike, Tyche

Script run (python3 fetch_eb1911.py); the article text is the tag-stripped parse output from the upper-case title onwards:

import html, json, re, time, urllib.parse, urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

OUT = Path(__file__).parent / "eb1911"
OUT.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
UA = "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)"
TITLES = ["Zeus", "Hera", "Poseidon", "Demeter", "Athena", "Apollo", "Artemis", "Ares", "Aphrodite",
          "Hephaestus", "Hermes", "Hestia", "Dionysus", "Hades", "Persephone", "Eros", "Cronus", "Helios",
          "Selene", "Eos", "Nike", "Tyche"]
summary = {}
for t in TITLES:
    page = f"1911 Encyclopædia Britannica/{t}"
    url = "https://en.wikisource.org/w/api.php?" + urllib.parse.urlencode(
        {"action": "parse", "page": page, "prop": "text", "format": "json", "formatversion": "2", "redirects": "1"})
    req = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": UA})
    d = json.load(urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=60))
    (OUT / f"{t}.json").write_text(json.dumps(d, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")
    if "error" in d:
        summary[t] = {"page": page, "error": d["error"]["info"]}
        continue
    text = re.sub(r"\s+", " ", html.unescape(re.sub(r"<[^>]+>", " ", d["parse"]["text"])))
    i = text.find(t.upper())
    summary[t] = {"page": d["parse"]["title"], "start": text[max(0, i): i + 900],
                  "roman": [m.group(0) for m in re.finditer(r".{0,150}(?:Roman|Latin|identified).{0,150}", text)][:5]}
    time.sleep(1)
(OUT / "summary.json").write_text(json.dumps(summary, indent=1, ensure_ascii=False), encoding="utf-8")

Review rounds 1–3: further 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica articles (the gods outside the Olympians are filed under their Latin names), and a re-fetch of the Olympian articles to read their contributors' signatures. Script eb.py, run as: python3 eb.py Proserpine Pluto Fortuna Fortune; python3 eb.py Zeus Hera Poseidon Demeter Athena Apollo Artemis Ares Aphrodite Hephaestus Hermes Hestia Dionysus; python3 eb.py Cupid Liber Luna Bacchus Orcus (Fortune and Orcus do not exist; Bacchus redirects to Dionysus; Luna has no relevant text).

UA = "solid-memo deck research (https://github.com/antwika/solid-memo)"

licensing: The deck is CC0 1.0. Its content comes from two sources whose licences allow anything: Wikidata, whose structured data is CC0, gave the correspondences, the English and Swedish names and most domains, and the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica, in the public domain (published 1910–1911, before 1931, in the US; elsewhere its articles used are anonymous or by contributors who died more than 70 years ago, see the source), gave the domains of Apollo and Persephone, the note on Dionysus and confirmation of the Roman names; facts and names are not copyrightable in any case, and the domain phrases are our own wording. The Theoi Project (all rights reserved) and Swedish Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0) were used only to verify facts: every answer and note rests on Wikidata or the 1911 Britannica, no prose was copied from them (the Athena answer "wisdom, war and crafts" coincides with a Theoi title line, but is a plain list of three domains all given by Wikidata), and the selection of gods is our own (the Olympians and the gods named in the editor's brief, plus five personified gods with a one-to-one Roman counterpart), not taken from any list on those sites. The modern Encyclopædia Britannica was not consulted (britannica.com refused the request) and nothing was taken from it.

rounds.lens: Machine checks against Wikidata and cross-checks of every card against the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica, the Theoi Project and Swedish Wikipedia
rounds.scope: All 43 cards, the property used for the correspondences, the Swedish names and the deck's licensing.
rounds.summary: The builder's Wikidata checks cover the English and Swedish labels or aliases of every Greek and Roman god named on the cards (except the Swedish name Dionysos, which Wikidata lacks), the P460 link from each Greek god to the Roman counterpart on the card, and P2925 values for the domains where Wikidata has them. Every correspondence agrees across Wikidata, Theoi and Swedish Wikipedia (and the 1911 Britannica for the Olympians). The discrepancies found and how they were resolved are listed below.

findings.issue: The brief pointed to P2959 for the correspondences; P2959 is "permanent duplicated item" and is not used between gods.
findings.resolution: Used P460 "said to be the same as", which is where Wikidata records Zeus = Jupiter and the other correspondences.

findings.issue: Wikidata Q41680 has no Swedish label; its only Swedish alias is the misspelling "Dinosys".
findings.resolution: Used "Dionysos", the title of the Swedish Wikipedia article (the name is also used in the Swedish Wikipedia article Bacchus). No Swedish label check for this god; the English label and P460 are checked. (Documentation corrected in round 3: "Dionysos" is the item's Swedish Wikipedia sitelink title as recorded in Wikidata, CC0, confirmed by the article.)

findings.issue: Wikidata's Swedish label of Sol (Q1199937) is "Sol Indiges"; "Sol" is an alias. Helios's P460 also lists Apollo-related and non-Roman sun gods.
findings.resolution: Used "Sol" (Swedish alias, the English label, Theoi's Roman name and the Latin name given in the Swedish Wikipedia article on Helios). Checked as a Swedish alias.

findings.issue: Wikidata P460 gives both Pluto and Dis Pater; Swedish Wikipedia says "Pluto och/eller Orcus"; the Swedish Wikipedia article on Pluto is titled "Pluton (mytologi)" and treats Pluton as the Greek title.
findings.resolution: Kept Pluto (Wikidata Swedish and English label, Theoi "Roman Pluto") and named Dis Pater in a note.

findings.issue: Wikidata P460 gives both Bacchus and Liber (and non-Roman gods); Theoi translates the name as "Liber, Bacchus".
findings.resolution: Kept Bacchus, the standard counterpart (Theoi title line "Roman Bacchus", Swedish Wikipedia "romarnas version av grekernas Dionysos"), and named Liber in a note.

findings.issue: Wikidata P460 gives Proserpina and Libera.
findings.resolution: Kept Proserpina (Theoi "Roman Name Proserpina"; Swedish Wikipedia: the Roman name of Persefone).

findings.issue: Wikidata P460 for Selene lists Luna and Diana; Swedish Wikipedia notes that Luna corresponds to Selene but is not related to her in origin.
findings.resolution: Kept Luna, the goddess who personifies the moon (Theoi "Roman Luna"); Diana is Artemis's counterpart.

findings.issue: The Roman god has two names, Cupid (Cupido) and Amor; Wikidata Q5011 has the English label "Cupid" and the Swedish label "Amor", and Swedish Wikipedia titles the article Amor.
findings.resolution: English answer Cupid, Swedish answer Amor, each language's established name, with the other name in a note.

findings.issue: Wikidata has no P2925 for Apollo and types him as a "solar deity"; the 1911 Britannica says he was wrongly identified with Helios in later times; Swedish Wikipedia calls him "ljusets, sjukdomens och konsternas gud".
findings.resolution: Answer "music, prophecy and healing" from the 1911 Britannica (confirmed by Theoi: prophecy, music, healing); the sun identification is mentioned as later in a note. No P2925 check.

findings.issue: Theoi calls Kronos "god of time", a meaning that comes from the ancient confusion of Kronos with Chronos; Swedish Wikipedia calls him a harvest god.
findings.resolution: No domain card for Cronus; only the uncontested correspondence with Saturn.

findings.issue: Wikidata's Tyche item (Q213440) is typed as an Oceanid and water deity, conflating the goddess of fortune with an Oceanid of the same name.
findings.resolution: The cards use only its labels, its P460 Fortuna and its description "Greek goddess of fortune", which agree with Theoi and Swedish Wikipedia; no check on P31.

findings.issue: The 1911 Britannica calls Hephaestus "analogous to, and by the ancients often confused with" Vulcan; Theoi notes Vulcanus was an original Italian god.
findings.resolution: The identification is nonetheless the standard one in all sources (Wikidata P460, Theoi "Roman Vulcan", Swedish Wikipedia); kept.

findings.issue: Wikidata P2925 also lists agriculture and pottery for Athena; Theoi lists many crafts.
findings.resolution: The answer keeps the main domains on which all sources agree (wisdom, war, crafts).

rounds.scope: All 43 cards, re-checked against Wikidata (P2925 of every god, the 136 builder checks), the 1911 Encyclopædia Britannica (Dionysus, Proserpine, Pluto, Demeter, Artemis), six Theoi Project pages and Swedish Wikipedia.
rounds.summary: No card was found wrong; all 22 correspondences and the Swedish names are the standard ones. Three warnings (the Pluto convention, and "spring growth" and "festivity" resting only on verification sources) and two suggestions (the god count in the description, a Hestia check). All five were verified against the sources and fixed.

findings.issue: Pluto is a Greek title of Hades in Latin form; the 1911 Britannica says the Romans usually called Hades Dis pater and Orcus, so the card should state the convention behind "Pluto".
findings.resolution: Verified in the 1911 Britannica "Pluto" ("Amongst the Romans Hades was usually called Dis pater ... and Orcus, although the name Pluto is often used") and Swedish Wikipedia (Pluton, Dis). Kept Pluto (Wikidata label and description "god in Roman religion, Plouton in Greek", P460, "often used" in the 1911 Britannica). The note now reads "Pluto comes from Plouton, a Greek name of Hades; the Romans also called him Dis Pater or Orcus." (sv likewise), written in our own words rather than the suggested text, which repeats Theoi's phrase "the Latin form of his Greek title Plouton". Added the 1911 Britannica "Pluto" and the Wikidata descriptions to the evidence.

findings.issue: "spring growth" is Theoi's exact phrase and no content source on the card supports it; the 1911 Britannica covers Persephone and Hades under "Proserpine" and "Pluto", which the method said did not exist.
findings.resolution: Verified: the articles exist under the Latin names (query 14). The back is now "the underworld and spring vegetation" / "underjorden och vårens växtlighet", from the 1911 Britannica "Proserpine" ("the growth of vegetation in spring", "goddess of the spring", queen "in the world below"), cited as content evidence; the article is also cited on persephone-roman, and "Pluto" on hades-domain and hades-roman. Method step 7 (query 7's purpose) corrected.

findings.issue: "festivity" comes only from Theoi's title line; no content source names it. Likewise "chance" on tyche-domain comes only from Theoi and Swedish Wikipedia.
findings.resolution: Verified: Wikidata P2925 gives only wine and winemaking, and the 1911 Britannica "Dionysus" says "god of wine and cheerfulness" and "ecstatic and mysterious rites" but not "festivity". The back is now "wine" / "vinet" with the note "Originally a god of vegetation, worshipped with ecstatic rites." (sv "Ursprungligen en växtlighetens gud, dyrkad med extatiska riter."), sourced from that article. tyche-domain: see round 3.

findings.issue: "the twelve Olympians with Hestia and Dionysus" reads as 12 + 2, so the stated total of 22 gods does not add up (the deck has 13 Olympian gods).
findings.resolution: Description now says "the twelve Olympians (counting both Hestia and Dionysus, as lists differ)" / "de tolv olympierna (både Hestia och Dionysos medräknade, eftersom listorna skiljer sig åt)".

findings.issue: Only "hearth" is checked; Wikidata also has P2925 dwelling (Q699405) for "home".
findings.resolution: Verified with SPARQL (query 15) and added the check Q41419 P2925 Q699405. The "sky" of zeus-domain stays covered by the Wikidata description and the 1911 Britannica, as the reviewer accepted.

rounds.reviewer: Claude (AI) — independent Language and translation reviewer
rounds.scope: All 43 cards in English and Swedish, plus the title, description and keywords.
rounds.summary: No Swedish name was found wrong and the language tags are right. One warning (definite and indefinite forms mixed in the Swedish domain answers) and five suggestions. Five were applied; the "Dis pater" spelling was declined.

findings.issue: Swedish domain answers mix definite and indefinite forms (Ares "kriget" against Athena "krig"); Swedish names a god's domain with a definite genitive, so the definite form reads most naturally.
findings.resolution: Verified against the Swedish Wikipedia intros ("vishetens och krigets gudinna", "kärlekens ... gudinna"). All Swedish domain answers now use the definite form: athena "visheten, kriget och hantverket", poseidon "havet, jordbävningarna och hästarna", apollo "musiken, spådomskonsten och läkekonsten", aphrodite "kärleken och skönheten", hermes "resenärerna, handeln och tjuvarna", eros "kärleken och åtrån"; the others already did. Method step 6 records the convention.

findings.issue: "vinet och festen" reads as one particular party, not the abstract sense of "festivity".
findings.resolution: The answer was cut to "wine" / "vinet" in round 1, so "festen" is gone.

findings.issue: "med hans eget namn" is not idiomatic; Swedish says "under ... namn".
findings.resolution: sv note now "Romarna övertog den grekiska guden under samma namn."

findings.issue: "Att han likställdes med solguden Helios kom senare." is clunky.
findings.resolution: sv note now "Först senare likställdes han med solguden Helios."

findings.issue: Swedish Wikipedia writes "Dis pater" or "Dispater", not "Dis Pater".
findings.resolution: Declined: Swedish usage varies. Wikidata's Swedish alias (Q1228338) is "Dis Pater" and the Swedish Wikipedia article Pluton (mytologi) also writes "Dis Pater" (query 16), while the article Dis (mytologi) writes "Dis pater". The note keeps "Dis Pater", as in the content source.

findings.issue: "the twelve Olympians with Hestia and Dionysus" can be read as 14 gods.
findings.resolution: Fixed with round 1's identical finding.

rounds.reviewer: Claude (AI) — independent Licensing, attribution and documentation reviewer
rounds.scope: All 43 cards' evidence (every quoted "says" string searched in re-fetched sources), the four sources' licences, the attribution in the deck and the report, and the method, queries and licensing text.
rounds.summary: The licences and attribution were found correct and every quote was found in its source. The problems were places where verification-only sources (Theoi, Swedish Wikipedia) had supplied wording or choices. All nine findings were verified and fixed (the athena-domain part of one needed only a documentation change). After this round every answer and note rests on Wikidata or the 1911 Britannica.

findings.issue: Error: "spring growth" is Theoi's wording and no content source supports it, against the licence policy and the dossier's own claims.
findings.resolution: Fixed as in round 1: new back "the underworld and spring vegetation" / "underjorden och vårens växtlighet", from the public-domain 1911 Britannica "Proserpine", which is now cited, and query 14 records its URL.

findings.issue: "wine and festivity" is Theoi's title line word for word, and "festivity" has no content source; athena-domain "wisdom, war and crafts" also matches a Theoi title, though Wikidata gives every element.
findings.resolution: Dionysus: answer cut to "wine" (Wikidata P2925) with a note from the 1911 Britannica (round 1). Athena: no card change, since wisdom and war are Wikidata P2925 values and crafts its P31 "deity of crafts"; the coincidence with Theoi's title line is now stated in the Theoi source entry and in the licensing paragraph instead of the earlier claim that nothing coincided.

findings.issue: "chance" rests only on Theoi and Swedish Wikipedia; Wikidata says "Greek goddess of fortune".
findings.resolution: Verified: no content source gives chance (Wikidata has no P2925 for Tyche; the 1911 Britannica has no Tyche article, and its "Fortuna" article even doubts that Fortuna stood for "the abstract idea of chance"). The back is now "fortune" / "lyckan", with the 1911 Britannica "Fortuna" added as evidence (also on tyche-roman).

findings.issue: Method step 4 let Theoi's title lines choose between two Roman counterparts, so a verification source made the selection.
findings.resolution: Verified the content sources settle each choice: rewrote step 4 to base them on Wikidata's descriptions (Pluto, Bacchus, Luna, Cupid) and the 1911 Britannica articles "Pluto", "Proserpine", "Cupid" and "Liber and Libera", Theoi being only confirmation. Added these to the evidence of hades-roman, persephone-roman, dionysus-roman, selene-roman and eros-roman.

findings.issue: The Swedish name "Dionysos" was documented as taken from a Swedish Wikipedia title, a verification-only source, though Wikidata's CC0 svwiki sitelink gives it.
findings.resolution: Verified (query 15: Q41680 svwiki sitelink "Dionysos"). Method step 5, the sv-wikipedia source entry, the round-0 finding and the card's Wikidata evidence now name the Wikidata sitelink as the source, confirmed by the article.

findings.issue: Queries 6 and 7 mention a Python script that is not recorded.
findings.resolution: The two scripts actually run are now pasted verbatim into queries 6 and 7 with the extraction rule; the review-round script is query 14.

findings.issue: The eb1911 licence evidence quotes only the US public-domain notice, while the deck is CC0 worldwide.
findings.resolution: Checked each article's signature (Wikisource header and initials) and the contributors' death years in Wikidata (query 15): Farnell d. 1934, Sikes d. 1940, Freese d. 1930, Frazer d. 1941, Fowler d. 1921; the other articles are unsigned. The licence evidence quotes the full notice and says this, and that only facts were taken.

findings.issue: The note "Companion of Aphrodite, in later myth her son" rests only on verification sources; the "son" part is in Wikidata P25 but not cited.
findings.resolution: Verified Q121973 P25 includes Q35500 (with other mothers, hence "in later myth"). Dropped "companion": the note is now "In later myth the son of Aphrodite." / "I senare myter Afrodites son.", with the Wikidata evidence and a P25 check. Also added the 1911 Britannica "Cupid" ("the god of love, Eros") as evidence.

findings.issue: Method step 7 and the eb1911 usedFor say the 1911 Britannica confirms every Olympian correspondence, but its Dionysus article names no Roman counterpart.
findings.resolution: Verified (it calls Bacchus a Thracian name of the god). Step 7 and usedFor now say so; the Roman identification comes from the 1911 Britannica "Liber and Libera" ("identified with the Greek Dionysus ... Liber (also called Liber Pater and Bacchus)"), now cited on dionysus-roman.

rounds.reviewer: Claude (AI) — independent Final re-check (loop 1): changed cards, every third card (facts and language), metadata, licence and documentation reviewer
rounds.lens: Final re-check (loop 1): changed cards, every third card (facts and language), metadata, licence and documentation
rounds.scope: 29 of the 43 cards (the 18 changed in round 3 and every third card), the metadata, the licence and the documentation; builder check and validate_sources.ts re-run.
rounds.summary: No errors or warnings; one suggestion, on eros-domain, which was verified and applied by shortening the answer to what the content sources state.

findings.issue: Suggestion: "desire" in "love and desire" / "kärleken och åtrån" has only indirect support in the content sources: Wikidata says "Greek god of love and sex" and has no P2925 for Eros, and the 1911 Britannica "Cupid" uses "desire" only as the meaning of the Latin name Cupido; only Theoi (verification only) names desire as Eros's domain.
findings.resolution: Verified: the wbgetentities description and the missing P2925 are as stated. Fetched the 1911 Britannica article "Eros (god)" (unsigned, query 17), which calls Eros "the god of love" and later "the capricious god of sexual passion", and gives Desire (Himeros) as a separate associate of Eros, so "desire" could even mislead. Shortened the answer to "love" / "kärleken", supported by Wikidata, the 1911 "Eros (god)" and "Cupid", Theoi and Swedish Wikipedia; added the "Eros (god)" article to the card's evidence and to the eb1911 source. The overlap with aphrodite-domain ("love and beauty") is one of meaning only and does not matter in a frontToBack deck; the backs remain unique.

front.en: What is Zeus the god of?

backNote.en: He is also the king of the gods.

evidence.says: Description "Greek god of the sky and king of the gods"; domain of saint or deity (P2925): lightning (Q33741), thunder (Q83301).
"His character and power as a deity of the sky, who ruled the phenomena of the air"; "the thunder was his most striking manifestation, and no doubt he was primevally a thunder-God".
"ZEUS was the King of the Gods and the god of the sky, weather, law and order, destiny and fate, and kingship."
Zeus "var gudarnas konung och himlens härskare i grekisk mytologi"; "Zeus attribut är en åskvigg".

front.en: What is Hera the goddess of?

backNote.en: She is also the queen of the gods, wife of Zeus.
backNote.sv: Hon är också gudarnas drottning, Zeus hustru.

evidence.says: Domain of saint or deity: mother, marriage (Q8445), childbirth, fertility. Zeus (Q34201) has spouse (P26) Hera.

"Hera was worshipped in two main capacities: (1) as the consort of Zeus and queen of heaven; (2) as the goddess who presided over marriage, and, in a wider sense, over the various phases of a woman's life."
"HERA was the Olympian queen of the gods, and the goddess of marriage, women, the sky and the stars of heaven."
"Hera ... var äktenskapets och fruktbarhetens gudinna i grekisk mytologi. Hon var gift med sin bror Zeus och var Olympens drottning."

front.en: What is Poseidon the god of?

evidence.says: Description "one of the twelve Olympians presiding over the sea, storms, earthquakes and horses"; P2925: sea (Q165), earthquake (Q7944), horse breeding (Q1265288).
"god of the sea and of water generally"; "Earthquakes were thought to be produced by Poseidon shaking the earth"; "The horse was especially associated with his worship".
"POSEIDON was the Olympian god of the sea, earthquakes, floods, drought and horses."
"Poseidon är havets, källornas, flodernas och jordbävningarnas gud i grekisk mytologi."

front.en: What is Demeter the goddess of?

evidence.says: Description "Greek goddess of the harvest, grains, and agriculture"; P2925: agriculture (Q11451), soil, fertility.
"DEMETER, in Greek mythology, daughter of Cronus and Rhea and sister of Zeus, goddess of agriculture and civilized life."
"DEMETER was the Olympian goddess of agriculture, grain and bread".
"Demeter ... var en fruktbarhets- och skördegudinna i grekisk mytologi".

front.en: What is Athena the goddess of?

backNote.en: In war she stands for strategy and the defence of cities, unlike Ares.
backNote.sv: I kriget står hon för strategi och städernas försvar, till skillnad från Ares.

evidence.says: Description "goddess of wisdom and war in ancient Greek religion and mythology"; instance of deity of wisdom, deity of crafts, war deity; P2925: war (Q198), wisdom (Q799), agriculture, pottery, weaving.

Athena: "In Homer Athena already appears as the goddess of counsel, of war, of female arts and industries, and the protectress of Greek cities". Ares: "As contrasted with Athena, who added to her other attributes that of being the goddess of well-conducted military operations, he personifies brute strength and the wild rage of conflict."
"Greek Goddess of Wisdom, War & Crafts"; "the Olympian goddess of wisdom and good counsel, war, the defence of towns, heroic endeavour, weaving, pottery and various other crafts".
"Athena eller Pallas Athena var vishetens och krigets gudinna i grekisk mytologi."

front.en: What is Apollo the god of?

backNote.en: His identification with the sun god Helios came later.
backNote.sv: Först senare likställdes han med solguden Helios.

evidence.says: "the idea of Apollo as a god of prophecy"; "Closely connected with the god of oracles was the god of the healing art"; "contributed to make Apollo a god of song and music, friend and leader of the Muses"; Delos was "the centre of the worship of the sun-god Helios, with whom Apollo was wrongly identified in later times".
No P2925 statement; instance of solar deity, Greek deity, Roman deity, Olympian god (labels en "Apollo", sv "Apollon").
"APOLLON (Apollo) was the Olympian god of prophecy and oracles, music, song and poetry, archery, healing, plague and disease, and the protection of the young."
"Han betraktas som ljusets, sjukdomens och konsternas gud."

front.en: What is Artemis the goddess of?

evidence.says: Description "goddess of the hunt and the wild in ancient Greek religion and mythology"; sv description "jaktens och kyskhetens gudinna samt beskyddare av kvinnor i grekisk mytologi".

"She is the daughter of Zeus and Leto, twin-sister and counterpart of Apollo"; "she is rather the patroness of the wild beasts of the field"; "The Greek Artemis was usually represented as a huntress with bow and quiver".
"ARTEMIS was the Olympian goddess of hunting, the wilderness and wild animals."
"Diana är i romersk mytologi de vilda djurens och jaktens gudinna. Hon kom att helt jämställas med grekernas gudinna Artemis."

front.en: What is Ares the god of?

backNote.en: Above all the violence of battle, unlike Athena.
backNote.sv: Framför allt stridens våld, till skillnad från Athena.

evidence.says: Description "Greek god of war and combat"; P2925: war (Q198); instance of war deity.
"ARES, in ancient Greek mythology, the god of war, or rather of battle"; "he personifies brute strength and the wild rage of conflict".
"ARES was the Olympian god of war, battlelust, courage and civil order."
"Ares ... var krigets, ursinnets och det besinningslösa våldets gud i grekisk mytologi."

front.en: What is Aphrodite the goddess of?

evidence.says: Domain of saint or deity: love (Q316, sv "kärlek"), beauty (Q7242, sv "skönhet").
"APHRODITE, the Greek goddess of love and beauty, counterpart of the Roman Venus."
"APHRODITE was the Olympian goddess of love, beauty, pleasure and procreation."
"Afrodite ... är kärlekens och fruktbarhetens gudinna"; "Afrodite var även skönhetens och familjelivets gudinna".

front.en: What is Hephaestus the god of?

evidence.says: Description "Greek god of blacksmiths"; P2925: fire (Q3196), volcano, forging (Q193057).
"HEPHAESTUS, in Greek mythology, the god of fire".
"HEPHAISTOS (Hephaestus) was the Olympian god of fire, smiths, craftsmen, metalworking, stonemasonry and sculpture."
"Hefaistos var i grekisk mytologi smideskonstens gud, som härskade över elden och vulkanerna."

front.en: What is Hermes the god of?

backNote.en: He is also the messenger of the gods and guides the dead to the underworld.
backNote.sv: Han är också gudarnas budbärare och leder de döda till underjorden.

evidence.says: Description: "the emissary and messenger of the gods; the god of trade, heraldry, merchants, commerce, roads, thieves, trickery, sports, travelers, and athletes"; P2925: trade (Q601401), thief (Q3562775), traveler (Q12356615).

"In the Odyssey, however, he appears mainly as the messenger of the gods, and the conductor of the dead to Hades"; "he was the protector of travellers"; "he became a deity of gain and commerce"; "From this conception his thievish character may have been evolved."

"HERMES was the Olympian god of herds and flocks, travellers and hospitality, roads and trade, thievery and cunning, ..."; "the herald and personal messenger of Zeus ... and also the guide of the dead who led souls down into the underworld."
"Hermes var i den grekiska mytologin gudarnas budbärare."; "han skyddade talare, köpmän och tjuvar".

front.en: What is Hestia the goddess of?

evidence.says: Description "Greek goddess of the hearth and the home"; P2925: hearth (Q585473), dwelling (Q699405), fire, cooking, baking.
"HESTIA, in Greek mythology, the 'fire-goddess,' daughter of Cronus and Rhea, the goddess of hearth and home."
"HESTIA was the virgin goddess of the hearth (both private and municipal) and the home."
Hestia "är i den grekiska mytologin hemmets och den husliga härdens evigt jungfruliga gudinna".

front.en: What is Dionysus the god of?

backNote.en: Originally a god of vegetation, worshipped with ecstatic rites.
backNote.sv: Ursprungligen en växtlighetens gud, dyrkad med extatiska riter.

evidence.says: Description "ancient Greek god of winemaking and wine"; P2925: wine (Q282), winemaking (Q213376).

"originally a nature god of fruitfulness and vegetation, especially of the vine; hence, distinctively, the god of wine."; "Dionysus may be regarded under two distinct aspects: that of a popular national Greek god of wine and cheerfulness, and that of a foreign deity, worshipped with ecstatic and mysterious rites introduced from Thrace."
"Greek God of Wine & Festivity"; "the Olympian god of wine, vegetation, pleasure, festivity, madness and wild frenzy."
Bacchus "var i romersk mytologi rusets och vinets gud. Han var romarnas version av grekernas Dionysos".

front.en: What is Hades the god of?

evidence.says: Description "god of the underworld in Greek mythology"; sv description "Grekisk gud över dödsriket och underjorden"; instance of death deity.
"PLUTO (Πλούτων), in Greek mythology, the god of the lower world. His oldest name was Hades"; "Here he ruled with his wife Persephone over the other powers below and over the dead."
"HAIDES (Hades) was the king of the underworld and god of the dead."
"Hades var i grekisk mytologi dödens gud och härskaren över underjorden"; "Som underjordens härskare styrde Hades över de döda".

front.en: What is Persephone the goddess of?

backNote.en: Queen of the underworld as the wife of Hades.

evidence.says: Description "Greek goddess of the seasons and the queen of the underworld; married with Hades".

Pluto "carried her off to be his queen in the world below"; of her spending part of each year with Pluto beneath the earth: "There can be little doubt that this is a mythological expression for the growth of vegetation in spring and its disappearance in autumn."; "As wife of Pluto, she sent spectres, ruled the ghosts"; "in her character of goddess of the spring she was honoured with flower-festivals in Sicily".
"PERSEPHONE was the goddess queen of the underworld, wife of the god Haides (Hades). She was also the goddess of spring growth".
Persefone: "Myten om Persefone och Demeter förklarar hur årstiderna uppstod." Proserpina: "Proserpina är underjordens drottning i den romerska mytologin" and identical with Persefone.

front.en: What is Eros the god of?

backNote.en: In later myth the son of Aphrodite.

evidence.says: Description "Greek god of love and sex"; sv description "kärleksguden i grekisk mytologi"; mother (P25): Aphrodite (Q35500), besides Nyx, Eris, Iris and Penia.
"EROS, in Greek mythology, the god of love."; later he became "the capricious god of sexual passion, the son of Aphrodite"; "The chief associates of Eros are Pothos and Himeros (Longing and Desire)".
"CUPID (Cupido, 'desire'), the Latin name for the god of love, Eros (q.v.)."
"Translation Love, Sexual Desire"; "EROS was the mischievous god of love, a minion and constant companion of the goddess Aphrodite"; some writers had him born of the goddess.
"Eros ... var en kärleksgud i grekisk mytologi. Han var son till Afrodite."

front.en: What is Helios the god of?

evidence.says: Description "Greek god and personification of the Sun"; P2925: Sun (Q525, sv "solen").
"HELIOS (Helius) was the Titan god of the sun, a guardian of oaths, and the god of sight."
Helios "tillhörde den grekiska mytologin och var en personifiering av solen."

front.en: What is Selene the goddess of?

evidence.says: Description "ancient Greek goddess and personification of the Moon"; P2925: Moon (Q405, sv "månen").
"SELENE was the Titan goddess of the moon."
"Selene är en mångudinna inom den grekiska mytologin."

front.en: What is Eos the goddess of?

evidence.says: Description "Greek goddess of the dawn"; P2925: dawn (Q11326182, sv "gryning"), red sky at morning (sv "morgonrodnad").
"EOS was the rosy-fingered goddess of the dawn."
"Eos är gryningens eller morgonrodnadens gudinna i grekisk mytologi".

front.en: What is Nike the goddess of?

evidence.says: Description "goddess of victory in Greek mythology"; P2925: victory (Q50000, sv "seger").
"NIKE (Nicé) was the winged goddess of victory--victory both in war and in peaceful competition."
Nike "är i grekisk mytologi segergudinnan".

front.en: What is Tyche the goddess of?

evidence.says: Description "Greek goddess of fortune"; her Roman counterpart Fortuna (Q4654) is "Roman goddess of fortune".

Fortuna "became more or less closely identified with the Gr. Τύχη, and was represented on coins, &c., with a cornucopia as the giver of prosperity, a rudder as the controller of destinies, and with a wheel, or standing on a ball, to indicate the uncertainty of fortune."
"TYKHE (Tyche) was the goddess of fortune, chance, providence and fate."
Tyche "är i den grekiska mytologin slumpens och i huvudsak den goda lyckans gudinna."
